messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have developed a Java application which does some computations and can 
then export numerical data to a CSV file. Now I would like to access the 
export class of this application directly from R. I am basically trying 
to get the data directly into R instead of doing this via a CSV file.

I suppose RJava can help me to achieve this goal. Unfortunately, I have 
encountered the following problem. I hope you can point me into the 
right direction.

In the Java class, the output is a two-dimensional array of type 
double[][]. I have managed to get one-dimensional arrays (i.e., 
double[]) from the Java application into R via the following command:

 > result <- .jcall(exportClass, "[D", "exportMethod")

But I have no clue how to replace "[D" by the correct return type for 
two-dimensional arrays. I tried "[[D", but it returns something like:

[[1]]
[1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@fd68b1"

[[2]]
[1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@e45076"

I have also found the method .jevalArray(), but .jevalArray(result) 
returns an error which says that the "object is not a Java object 
reference (jobjRef/jarrayRef)". I don't know if this is the right method 
anyway.

I would appreciate any hints. Thank you!

Philip

messages.subject: Re: JGR licence change request
messages.body_plain:
Illhami,

Though I am on the author list, the vast majority of JGR is the work of the other developers. I will support any changes that they wish to make.

Personally I have become more and more concerned about the overreaching nature of the claims that the FSF makes about the GPL. In particular their claims that the calling of any function in a GPL'ed program implies that your program is not a separate program, but in fact part (i.e. a derivative work of) of the GPL'ed program.  I believe that this claim is on shaky legal ground, and limits the freedom of third party developers to do what they wish with code that they have written themselves.

A move to LGPL, MIT or BSD would solve Illhami's problem, and would make JGR a more open platform.

Thoughts?

Best,
Ian

messages.subject_clean: Cost of a function with a [[B return signature
messages.body_plain:
Hello

I have a Java method:

public byte[][] content(){
       return(contents); //(1)
       // return(null);  //(2)
}

which I call from R as:

.jcall(f,"[[B","content") //(A)

a 1000 times. This takes ~27 seconds to run.
If I comment out (1) and uncomment (2), it takes 2.3 seconds.
The total size of the double array returned in (A) is 304 bytes.
There is no other processing done after (A).

The mean time per call of (A) is roughly 0.025 seconds.

Is there a faster way to return double byte arrays (to R) in rJava?

Regards

Saptarshi

messages.subject_clean: Cost of a function with a [[B return signature
messages.body_plain:
On Nov 17, 2010, at 4:35 AM, Saptarshi Guha wrote:

> Hello
> 
> I have a Java method:
> 
> public byte[][] content(){
>       return(contents); //(1)
>       // return(null);  //(2)
> }
> 
> which I call from R as:
> 
> .jcall(f,"[[B","content") //(A)
> 
> a 1000 times. This takes ~27 seconds to run.
> If I comment out (1) and uncomment (2), it takes 2.3 seconds.
> The total size of the double array returned in (A) is 304 bytes.
> There is no other processing done after (A).
> 
> The mean time per call of (A) is roughly 0.025 seconds.
> 
> Is there a faster way to return double byte arrays (to R) in rJava?
> 

The issue is not returning the array, but all conversions involved. The default for .jcall is evalArray = TRUE so the result is converted in R into a list of Java objects which is where your penalty is. Using evalArray = FALSE will reduce the conversions.

That said, it really depends on what you're up to -- passing Java arrays of more than 1 dimension is in general not a good idea, because typically you'll have to convert them into R vectors anyway (remember - arrays in R are 1d-vectors!) and that conversion is much faster in Java.

[as a side note that is something that may be called a bug in that .jcall even with evalArray=FALSE calls newArray with simplify=TRUE which is not necessarily intended but there is no corresponding conversion API for the "fixed" case so that will need some discussion... hint@Romain ;)]

Cheers,
Simon

In particular their claims that the calling of any function in a GPL'ed program implies that your program is not a separate program, but in fact part (i.e. a derivative work of) of the GPL'ed program.  I believe that this claim is on shaky legal ground, and limits the freedom of third party developers to do what they wish with code that they have written themselves.
>> 
>> A move to LGPL, MIT or BSD would solve Illhami's problem, and would make JGR a more open platform.
>> 
> 
> Well, there are people that would argue the opposite - it would make it far more closed as it would remove the obligation for modifications to be shared.
> 
> The reason JGR is GPL v2 is that the usual "GPL x and higher" clause opens us to the whims of the FSF in the future and the GPL v3 controversy is a good example why we don't want that.
> 
> As for the original request, I agree that with Ian that the intention of JGR (and R as well) is that packages are free to extend it so if you want to write a package it is independent of the license of JGR as long as you don't need to modify JGR to do so (i.e., if you don't modify JGR you're not creating a derivative work so the license is irrelevant to you as it doesn't cover use --- and the API is publicly available without the need for source code license).


Actually, this is precisely what the FSF claims. see the faq at: http://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#LinkingWithGPL. Even more specifically dealing with java, the fsf says:
"
It has always been the FSF's position that dynamically linking applications to libraries creates a single work derived from both the library code and the application code. The GPL requires that all derivative works be licensed under the GPL, an effect which can be described as “hereditary.” So, if an application links to a library licensed under the GPL, the application too must be licensed under the GPL. By contrast, libraries licensed under the GNU Lesser General Public License (LGPL) may be linked to proprietary applications.

(...snip...)

The typical arrangement for Java is that each library an application uses is distributed as a separate JAR (Java Archive) file. Applications use Java's “import” functionality to access classes from these libraries. When the application is compiled, function signatures are checked against the library, creating a link. The application is then generally a derivative work of the library. So, the copyright holder for the library must authorize distribution of the work. The LGPL permits this distribution.
"
http://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-java.html

So if javaClass.java contains the line:
import x;
Then (according to the FSF) javaClass.java is a derivative work of x. If x is GPL'ed, then javaClass.java must be GPL'ed. if x is LGPL'ed, the javaClass.java can have any license.

In fact the restriction that linked programs must be GPL'ed is the primary difference between GPL and LGPL. Whether this is legally enforceable, or even implied by the GPL license its self is a matter of some debate. When Richard Stallman came to UseR! this year I asked him if there was likely to be a court case involving this issue anytime in the near future so that it can be settled by a court of law. He said that there were no 'illegal linking' cases that were on the horizon.

It seems to me that the LGPL unambiguously functions the way that you want, with modifications of JGR's code needing to be shared, and linking allowed.

messages.subject: Re: Cost of a function with a [[B return signature
messages.subject_clean: Cost of a function with a [[B return signature
messages.body_plain:
I'm returning an array of byte arrays. These byte arrays correspond to
serialized R objects.
My approach (now) is to flatten it out : length of serialized bytes,
serialized bytes,....
pass 1D array to R and deserialize from there.  Great speed
improvements but not enough.

Thanks
Saptarshi


On Wed, Nov 17, 2010 at 8:00 AM, Romain Francois
<romain.francois at dbmail.com> wrote:
> Le 17/11/10 16:48, Simon Urbanek a écrit :
>>
>>
>> On Nov 17, 2010, at 4:35 AM, Saptarshi Guha wrote:
>>
>>> Hello
>>>
>>> I have a Java method:
>>>
>>> public byte[][] content(){
>>>       return(contents); //(1)
>>>       // return(null);  //(2)
>>> }
>>>
>>> which I call from R as:
>>>
>>> .jcall(f,"[[B","content") //(A)
>>>
>>> a 1000 times. This takes ~27 seconds to run.
>>> If I comment out (1) and uncomment (2), it takes 2.3 seconds.
>>> The total size of the double array returned in (A) is 304 bytes.
>>> There is no other processing done after (A).
>>>
>>> The mean time per call of (A) is roughly 0.025 seconds.
>>>
>>> Is there a faster way to return double byte arrays (to R) in rJava?
>>>
>>
>> The issue is not returning the array, but all conversions involved. The
>> default for .jcall is evalArray = TRUE so the result is converted in R into
>> a list of Java objects which is where your penalty is. Using evalArray =
>> FALSE will reduce the conversions.
>>
>> That said, it really depends on what you're up to -- passing Java arrays
>> of more than 1 dimension is in general not a good idea, because typically
>> you'll have to convert them into R vectors anyway (remember - arrays in R
>> are 1d-vectors!) and that conversion is much faster in Java.
>>
>> [as a side note that is something that may be called a bug in that .jcall
>> even with evalArray=FALSE calls newArray with simplify=TRUE which is not
>> necessarily intended but there is no corresponding conversion API for the
>> "fixed" case so that will need some discussion... hint@Romain ;)]
>>
>> Cheers,
>> Simon

messages.subject: Java on Mac OS X 10.6.5 (Snow Leopard)
messages.subject_clean: Java on Mac OS X 10.6.5 (Snow Leopard)
messages.body_plain:
Apparently the latest update to Snow Leopard (10.6.5) removes necessary header files from the system Java installation. They are now only available in the corresponding Xcode SDKs. What does that mean?


* If you are using binaries from CRAN, there is nothing to worry about and you can ignore this e-mail.



* If you are compiling packages against the JavaVM from sources (such as rJava), you will need to point the compilers to the new location of the headers.

For example if you want to use the 10.6 SDK you'll have to use:
JAVA_CPPFLAGS=-I/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX10.6.sdk/System/Library/Frameworks/JavaVM.framework/Headers

You have two options: you can re-run javareconf with JAVA_CPPFLAGS specified, i.e. (the command is all on one line!):
JAVA_CPPFLAGS=-I/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX10.6.sdk/System/Library/Frameworks/JavaVM.framework/Headers R CMD javareconf

this will configure R with the correct flags. Alternatively, you can set JAVA_CPPFLAGS before installing the packages in question if you don't want to touch the R Java configuration.

Note: the above assumes you installed Xcode in the default location "/Developer" - adjust accordingly if you used a custom location.


Cheers,
Simon
